subject: Chemistry
topic: Why KMnO₄ is so intensely coloured
title: No d Electrons, Still Purple: Why KMnO₄ Is So Intensely Coloured
summary: In MnO₄⁻ manganese is +7 (3d⁰), so no d–d transition is possible. The colour comes from ligand-to-metal charge transfer: visible light moves an electron from an oxygen into the empty d orbitals of Mn. This absorbs green-yellow light (≈ 525 nm), so the solution looks purple. Charge transfer is an allowed transition, so it absorbs far more light than restricted d–d transitions: KMnO₄ is intensely coloured while Ti³⁺(aq) or Mn²⁺(aq) are pale. Chromate (yellow) and dichromate (orange), also d⁰, are coloured the same way.

notes.title: 16 – Why KMnO₄ Is So Intensely Coloured (Charge Transfer)

keyPoints: In MnO₄⁻, Mn is **+7 (3d⁰)**: no d–d transition is possible.
Light moves an electron from **O to the empty d orbitals of Mn**: **ligand-to-metal charge transfer**.
It absorbs **green-yellow** (≈ 525 nm); red + blue left over look **purple**.
Charge transfer is **allowed**, d–d is **restricted**: so KMnO₄ is far more intensely coloured. CrO₄²⁻ and Cr₂O₇²⁻ (d⁰) too.

blocks.p: d–d bands: molar absorptivity ε ≲ 100 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. MnO₄⁻: ε ≈ 3 × 10³ L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹ at 525 nm (tens to hundreds of times stronger).
Oxidation state of Mn in KMnO₄: +1 + x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +7; Mn⁷⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁰. The purple colour therefore cannot be d–d; it is O → Mn charge transfer absorbing green-yellow light.
